MGT409 AI Foundations · Final project · Fall 2026

Grant Compass

Grant Compass is an AI development team for small nonprofits: it finds grants that fit, tells you honestly whether to apply, and helps you write answers that are true to your own records.

1 · MOTIVATIONI was the person this is for

Before business school, I was a fundraiser. I joined to help a mission I believed in, and found that most of my week went to paperwork instead.

Grant season meant scrolling through foundation websites to work out whether we were even eligible, then rebuilding the same answers from last year's applications for a new funder's word limits. Before anything went out, I had to hunt through program reports to confirm that every number I had written was actually true, because one wrong statistic in front of a funder costs more than one lost grant. After an award came the reports, and after that the board update. Every deadline landed in the same weeks as program work, so the applications that got submitted were the ones I had time for, not always the ones we were best placed to win.

None of that work is what a funder pays for or what a community needs from us. It is the cost of being heard. Grant Compass is the tool I wanted in that job.

Who has this problem

About 1.9 million registered nonprofits in the US, most of them running on under $1 million a year. In those organisations, grant work falls on one or two people (a development director, an executive director, a program manager writing at night) who also run the programmes the grants pay for.

How they handle it today

  • A spreadsheet of deadlines, and funder websites searched one by one, or a paid database for those who can afford one.
  • Copying and editing paragraphs from old applications.
  • Increasingly, pasting questions into ChatGPT, which writes fluently but can state numbers that aren't in the organisation's records.
  • For those with budget, a freelance grant writer for each important proposal.
Grant Compass · Gabriella SavenMotivation · 2 / 15

What it costs: money, time and frustration

68%of organisations name time as their biggest grant-seeking challenge (GrantStation, 2023)
2 days–4 weeksto prepare a single proposal (SSIR, on grant-writing workloads)
~48 hoursmedian time per application to a philanthropic funder (SmartyGrants)
$1,500–$5,000a freelance writer's flat fee for one full foundation proposal; hourly rates are $30–150 (Grantable, 2026)
22% vs 72%of very small vs other nonprofits received even one foundation grant (Candid)
$299+/monthfor a grant-search database like Instrumentl, out of reach for most small groups

Time: dozens of hours per application, mostly searching, re-formatting and fact-checking rather than thinking. Money: either staff hours taken from programmes, or fees a small budget can't carry. Frustration: the work is repetitive, deadlines collide, and the people doing it know the hours came out of the mission. Candid's data shows the result: the smallest organisations, often closest to their communities, are the least likely to win foundation money at all.

Why care

Because every hour belongs to the community. A fundraiser's time is one of the scarcest resources a small nonprofit has, and right now too much of it goes to searching, re-typing and double-checking. Grant Compass is about optimising our time for the communities we serve: software does the searching, the first draft and the fact-check; people spend their hours on the work only they can do, building relationships with funders and showing up for the families, veterans and students who rely on them.

Better-targeted applications also mean the money is more likely to arrive. When a two-person team can apply to the right five funders instead of the nearest two, that is more meals, more tutoring hours, more veterans housed.

“It feels like it was designed by someone who actually understands how grant fundraising works rather than just adding AI onto a generic CRM.”

2 · WHAT IS NEW HERENot a grant database, and not a chatbot

What already exists

Finds grantsJudges fit against your documentsDrafts answersChecks claims against your recordsAfter the awardPrice
Instrumentl✓ large databaseKeyword matchAI assist (higher tiers)—Tracking (top tier)$299–$999/mo
Candid Foundation Directory✓ reference database————≈$1,200–$2,200/yr
Grantable (startup)Basic—✓ AI drafting——$0–$150/mo
ChatGPT—Only what you paste✓— can invent numbers—$0–$20/mo
Freelance writerSometimes✓ (human)✓✓ (human)Extra fee$1,500–$5,000 flat fee per proposal (≈$75/h)
Grant Compass✓ Grants.gov, state portals, 74 foundations, any link✓ 7 dimensions, quotes verified✓ from your documents only✓ Evidence Checker + Coach✓ reports, board update≈$0.19/mo in AI

What is different, honestly

Instrumentl and Candid are better databases, and a good freelance writer is better at prose. What is new is the combination, built around one rule: the AI may only say what your own records support, and code, not the AI, checks that it did.

  • A team that checks itself. Seven agents with narrow jobs; two exist only to check the others (the Evidence Checker and the Executive Director). In the traced run, the checker caught the writer's mistake.
  • Verification in code. Fit % and eligibility are computed, not asked for; quotes must match the source word for word; the Director's claims must match real metrics. Generic AI tools trust the model.
  • Honest go / no-go. The Fit Agent will say Research further or No-Go, uses your history with the funder, and explains every score with quotes.
  • The whole life cycle, from search to funder report to board update, in one place.
“The Grant Coach feels much more useful than just asking ChatGPT to rewrite something because it actually tells you what is missing, whether you’ve answered the question properly and where the evidence is weak.”

A friend with grant-fundraising experience, after trying the app

Why the difference matters

For a small nonprofit, a wrong number in an application can cost a funder relationship that took years to build, so speed without verification is a bad trade. And at under 20 cents a month in AI costs, this can be offered to the organisations that can't justify $300 a month, the ones Candid's data shows are left out.

3 · THE AGENTSSeven colleagues with narrow jobs

How they are organised, and who hands work to whom

work handed onfacts read from your librarysupervision (metrics only)a human decision

Work moves left to right like a real development team. Research reads a funder and hands the extracted facts to Fit, which scores them against your library. You decide Go / No-Go. The Writer drafts each answer, then the Coach and Evidence Checker review it in parallel, and you approve what is sent. A person sits at the two decisions that matter: whether to apply, and what to send.

The Executive Director supervises from above. It sees only metrics (failure rates, quote-warning rates, costs), never documents, so it can't be manipulated by them. The Compass Assistant is a read-only chat layer over everything. Agents don't call each other: the app passes each one exactly the inputs it needs, and each returns a typed result (a Pydantic model), so code can check it.

Models used, and why

Every call uses gpt-6-luna through Portkey (the course key), with low reasoning effort, a 6,000-token output cap, and at most 6 model calls and 120,000 tokens per run. A small, cheap model is enough because the hard parts (scores, eligibility, quote matching, totals) are done in code; the model only reads and writes. Section 4 tests whether more reasoning would help: it cost 58% more and did not.

One real run, traced step by step

Sunday 25 October 2026, on the Cedar Ridge Veterans Collaborative (a demo organisation in San Antonio). All screenshots are from this run; token counts are from the app's usage log.

1 · Paste a real funder link

On Discover, the Cedar Ridge Veterans Collaborative (a San Antonio demo organisation) pastes the San Antonio Area Foundation's real grants page. The Research Agent reads the live page and extracts the open programme (Special and Urgent Needs, rolling deadline). No application questions were on the page, and it says so.

Research Agent · 3,628 input (0 cached) · 294 output · $0.0006 · 1.16 s

2 · Fit assessment

The Fit Agent scores 59%: Geography 5/5 (the foundation funds Bexar County, where Cedar Ridge works), Funding size and Effort unknown because the page doesn't state them, and recommends Research further rather than Go. The code marks it 'Filtered out' too, because the page also says several 2026 programmes are closed: the app is honest that this is not a sure thing.

Fit Agent · 7,719 input (0 cached) · 1,757 output · $0.0018 · 11.61 s

Grant Compass · Gabriella SavenAgents · 7 / 15

3 · You decide, add a question, Draft with AI

The user clicks Add & start application, pastes the funder's question (250-word limit) and clicks Draft with AI. In 6 seconds the Grant Writer returns 174 words built only from Cedar Ridge's documents: 318 of 412 households housed in 2025-26, the Homeward Navigation programme, the family make-up of the current cohort.

Grant Writer · 5,314 input (0 cached) · 885 output · $0.0011 · 6.18 s

4 · Review suggestions (Grant Coach)

Switching to Review suggestions runs the Coach in the background. It scores the draft 65/100 ('Getting there'), checks each part of the question (all three only partly answered), and underlines six passages. Clicking one opens a suggestion card: Urgency lacks evidence, with why it matters and Accept / Reject.

Grant Coach · 2,982 input (0 cached) · 1,677 output · $0.0012 · 10.05 s

5 · Check evidence

The Evidence Checker tests 12 claims against the documents: 7 Supported, 2 Weakly supported, 1 Needs evidence and 2 Contradicted. The writer had labelled first-quarter 2026 cohort figures (41% families with children, 38% with a disability rating) as 2025-26 results; the checker caught it and shows the source passage. This is the team working as designed: one agent's mistake is caught by another before a funder sees it.

Evidence Checker · 3,983 input (0 cached) · 1,079 output · $0.0010 · 6.36 s

Whole run: 23,626 input and 5,692 output tokens across five agents, $0.0058, about 40 seconds of AI time. One step was wrong (the Writer's dates) and another agent caught it before a human had to.

UsersAI cost per monthAI cost per year

Even at five times the heavy-user assumption, 10,000 users would cost about $9,366 a month in AI. At that scale hosting, support and data costs dominate; the AI itself stays small, which is what makes a low price for very small nonprofits plausible.

What we did to cut cost

  • Code before AI. Keyword and rule-based triage filters search results first (115 of the traced search's results were filtered out at no cost); only the rest get a Fit assessment.
  • Never pay twice. Foundation pages are hashed and re-read by the AI only when their text changes; earlier assessments are reused ("18 from earlier searches (no cost)").
  • Cache-friendly prompts. Instructions and the organisation's library come first, in a stable order, so the provider serves them from cache at a tenth of the price.
  • Small model, low reasoning, hard caps on output tokens, requests and total tokens per run.
Grant Compass · Gabriella SavenTokenomics · 10 / 15

Did the cuts hurt performance? An experiment

The Fit Agent assessed the same six Cedar Ridge grants three ways: 18 real runs, logged separately so the app's own health figures were untouched (report/cost_experiment.py).

Setting (same 6 grants)Avg inputCachedAvg outputAvg costAvg timeSame Go/No-Go as shippedAvg fit gap vs shippedQuote warnings
A · Shipped: low reasoning, library first (cacheable)4,86288%1,537$0.00099.6 s6/6—1
B · Library after the grant (no shared prefix)4,8620%1,475$0.00138.2 s4/62.5 pts1
C · Medium reasoning effort4,86274%2,400$0.001413.9 s3/63.7 pts0
A · Shipped$0.88 per 1,000 assessments
B · No cache-friendly order$1.34 per 1,000 assessments
C · Medium reasoning$1.39 per 1,000 assessments

Caching works and costs nothing in quality. With the instructions and library first, 88% of input tokens came from cache (versus 0%), cutting the cost per assessment by 35%. The prompt content is identical, so any difference in answers is the model's own run-to-run variation.

More reasoning cost +58% and was 4 s slower, without better decisions. Fit scores moved by 3.7 points on average. Recommendations matched the shipped setting on 3 of 6 grants, but setting B, which reasons exactly like A, matched on only 4 of 6: on borderline grants the model flips between Research further and No-Go whatever the setting. (High fit with No-Go is expected here: those grants are due in 1–4 days or already submitted.) So low reasoning stays, and the variability is listed as a limit in section 7. Six grants is a small sample: evidence, not proof.

Conclusion. Caching is a free saving. Low reasoning effort is enough for this task; spending more did not make the agent's decisions better or more consistent. The real quality risk is run-to-run variation on borderline grants, which is now listed as a limit with a planned fix.

Defenses working in the app

Overspending guards

Every run is capped at 6 model calls, 120,000 tokens and 6,000 output tokens. Messages over 2,000 characters and libraries over 120,000 characters are refused before any AI call, and uploads over 10 MB before they are read. Agent health shows each agent's runs, cost and failures, and the Executive Director flags anything unusual.

6 · IMPACTHours back for the communities we serve

A real user

A friend with grant-fundraising experience tried the app on their own in October 2026 and sent me an honest review (full text in report/user_review.md).

“It gets to the part that takes so much time in fundraising, which is working out whether something is actually worth pursuing before you sink hours into an application.”
“I could genuinely see this saving a lot of time for a small fundraising team, especially where one person is juggling research, deadlines and writing at the same time.”
“It actually feels like something I would use in real life, which I wasn’t expecting from a student project.”
“The pipeline is probably my favourite bit. Being able to see deadlines, risk, funding amount, where each application is at and what the next action is all in one place is genuinely helpful.”

What they'd improve: “keep pushing the organisation knowledge/evidence side because that is where I think it becomes especially valuable.” It is now one of the next steps on page 15.

What it adds up to

A careful estimate, to be tested by the user session: if a development director saves even 5 hours per application on research, first drafts and fact-checking, four applications a month returns about 20 hours a month, half a work week, to programmes and funder relationships. Newly possible: a two-person nonprofit can screen dozens of funders a month and fact-check every answer, which today only organisations with a paid database and a dedicated grants team can do.

7 · LIMITS AND NEXT STEPSWhat doesn't work yet

  • Coverage. 74 foundation websites can be read automatically; many funders publish only through JavaScript portals or PDFs behind logins, and Texas and many other states have no open grants feed.
  • The writer still makes mistakes, as the trace shows. The checker catches them, but a person must read the result. The app never submits anything.
  • Borderline recommendations vary. Asked twice about the same grant, the Fit Agent sometimes says Research further once and No-Go the next. Fit scores are stable to a few points; the label isn't.
  • Quote checks are strict. About a third of Fit assessments carry a quote that doesn't match word for word (often a profile that changed since). The app shows these as warnings rather than hiding them.
  • Local only. No hosting or shared team logins, and the login lockout is kept in memory. A real deployment needs hosting, backups and a legal review of the privacy policy.
  • Fictional demo data. The six organisations are realistic but invented.

With another month

  • Pilot with two or three real nonprofits and measure hours saved and win rate over a full grant cycle.
  • Run the Fit Agent twice on borderline grants and show "uncertain" when the runs disagree.
  • Read funder portals and PDFs behind links; add more state feeds and community foundations.
  • Deepen the organisation-knowledge side, as the user review suggested: guided prompts to fill evidence gaps the Evidence Checker finds, and outcome data that updates the library after every report.
  • Learn from outcomes: feed funders' feedback on losses back into Fit scores and the Coach.
  • Host it, with shared team accounts, roles, and a record of who approved each answer.
